response.evidence: These figures are approximate, from a manual review of the rows rather than an exact computed tally. The large majority of White male applicants in the dataset had loans originated. Their denial rate (about 14 denials, roughly 7%) is similar to or lower than the overall denial rate and the rates for other groups. Hispanic or Latino, Asian, White female and Black applicants were all denied at similar or higher rates. Most White male denials share risk factors seen in denials across all groups: debt-to-income ratios of 50%-60% or above 60% (e.g., 865k, 485k, 315k, 45k, 935k, 945k, 35k loans), reported income of 0 (255k and 725k loans), or very small loans with low income. Many White male applicants with DTI below 50% and standard loan-to-value ratios were approved. Applicants of every race with DTI above 60% were also mostly denied. The pattern is consistent with decisions driven by debt-to-income and income, not race or sex. Limitations: this data cannot explain any single decision, and it lacks credit score and other underwriting factors, so it can neither prove nor rule out discrimination in your individual case. A lender is generally required to tell you the principal reasons for a denial, so you can request them; if they seem inconsistent with your finances, you can file a complaint with the CFPB.
